sentences.text: The boar came through the hedge at the same place every night, and there was no place in the hedge.
Sabela had checked.

She had checked in daylight with her hands, working along the bottom of it from the gatepost to the corner, pushing her arm in up to the shoulder where the blackthorn allowed and taking it out again scratched.
The hedge at that point was two hundred years of blackthorn grown into itself, laid twice by somebody who knew how, and packed at the base with bramble that would have stopped a dog.
At about ten past nine, most nights, the boar came through it as though it were a doorway.
She had seen him first in April, from the bathroom window, and had assumed he had come round the end.
In May she watched properly, with the light off, and he did not come round the end.

He came out of the hedge at the third fence post, walked diagonally across the top of the vegetable garden without touching a single thing in it, went along the wall, and left through the far hedge at a point where there was also no gap.
He was enormous and he was old.
The bristles along his back had gone grey at the tips and there was a notch out of his left ear the size of a coin.
He never hurried and he never looked at the house.
What bothered her was the diagonal.
If you are an animal crossing a garden, you cross it.
You go where it is easy and you leave where you can.
He did not do that.

He walked a line — a specific line, the same line, so exactly the same that by June there was a faint pale track worn across the top bed where nothing would grow — and the line did not correspond to anything.
It went past the shed at a distance of about a metre and a half.
It went between the two apple trees and not around them.
It crossed the wall at a place where the wall was highest, and he went over it there, heavily, when there was a low bit twelve metres to the left.
Sabela was eleven and she was extremely interested in things that did not make sense, which her mother described as a phase and her grandfather described, more accurately, as a personality.
The interest had a shape, and the shape was always the same.
She did not want an explanation.

She wanted the thing to go on being odd for as long as possible while she found out more about it, and she had learned by about nine that if you take a strange thing to an adult too early they hand you back an ordinary one and are pleased with themselves.
So she did not tell anybody about the boar for two months.
She started marking the line.
She put a stone at the fence post, a stone at the shed, a stone between the apple trees, a stone at the wall.
When she had four stones down she stood at the gatepost and looked along them, and they made a road.
Not a path.
A road: straight, purposeful, wide enough for a cart, going from somewhere behind the hedge to somewhere over the wall.
It went through the vegetable garden the way a road goes through a field, which is to say without any interest in the field at all.
She went in and asked her grandfather whether there had ever been a road across the top garden.
He was doing the crossword and he did not look up for a while.
Then he said: "Which way was it going?" Which was, she thought afterwards, an extraordinary way to answer a question about whether something exists.
